lead.kicker: TOP STORY  •  THE UNITED STATES AND IRAN
lead.headline: Trump Declares an Economic D-Day on Iran
lead.deck: The president promised economic warfare on an unprecedented scale, and warned that any country giving Iran a lifeline would pay a price of its own.
body: The message went up on Truth Social on Wednesday evening. Iran had failed to take its chance at a deal, President Trump wrote, and would now face "economic warfare and isolation on an unprecedented scale". He called it an ECONOMIC D-DAY. No new rule was published and no names were listed, only a promise of harder squeezing.

The threat that mattered was aimed at everyone else. Any country whose banks, businesses, airports or government offices give Iran "any type of lifeline" will face tremendous consequences, he wrote, listing what must stop: oil smuggling, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, front companies. Sanctions are rules one country writes about who may trade with another, and they only bite if the rest of the world follows them.

Some of the world was already following. Hours earlier the United Arab Emirates, long Iran's most useful trading neighbour, froze all financial ties with Tehran, saying two Iranian missiles had fallen near its waters. Iran denied firing them. Brent crude rose above $93 a barrel.

map.title: IRAN AND ITS NEAREST MARKET
map.footnote: About 150 km of Gulf water between Bandar Abbas and Dubai
map.caption: The nearest place to do business has just stopped doing business.

lead.why: Sanctions are not a wall. They are a request. Washington can forbid American banks from touching Iranian money, but it cannot forbid an Emirati bank or a Chinese refinery. What it can do is make the choice painful: trade with Iran, or trade with the United States, but not both. Because almost every large bank in the world needs access to dollars, that choice usually goes one way. The UAE moving first, and China so far refusing to move at all, is this whole policy in miniature. It is also why sanctions work slowly. They do not stop a country doing things. They raise the cost of everything it does, and then wait.

world.headline: The Fastest Ebola Outbreak Ever Recorded
world.deck: Congo's health ministry has counted 5,021 cases and 2,378 deaths. The head of the World Health Organization says the epidemic is far from under control.
body: Congo's Ebola outbreak passed 5,000 cases on Wednesday. Government figures showed 5,021 infections and 2,378 deaths, and the WHO's director-general, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said on Tuesday that the epidemic "is far from being under control". Measured from its first known case, it has spread about three times faster than the West African epidemic of 2014 to 2016, which killed more than 11,000 people and is still the deadliest on record.

Two things make this one harder to stop. The virus is a rare strain called Bundibugyo, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment, so the tool that ended earlier outbreaks does not exist here. And it is burning through Ituri, a province in the far northeast where armed groups operate, roads are bad and many thousands have been driven from home. Nearly half of those who catch it are dying. In North Kivu the figure is seven in ten.
Trust is the other missing tool. On Monday a crowd in Aru attacked a health team sent to check a suspected case, burning an ambulance. Some nurses have gone on strike after months without pay.

illustration.title: FIVE THOUSAND CASES
illustration.subtitle: Eastern Congo
illustration.caption: A vaccine exists for one kind of Ebola. Not for this one.

world.connect: Ebola is not new to Congo. The virus was identified there in 1976 and named after a river, and the country has lived through more than a dozen outbreaks since. What is new is the speed, and speed in an epidemic is mostly about people rather than biology. A virus that spreads only through contact with a sick person's body fluids ought to be containable. It becomes uncontainable when the sick cannot reach a clinic, when the clinic has no beds, when families wash and bury their own dead, and when the figures arriving in protective suits are strangers who cannot explain themselves in the local language. That is why outbreak responders end up talking less about medicine than about roads, wages and trust.

india.headline: A War in the Gulf Reaches the Indian Kitchen
india.deck: With cooking gas dearer and harder to ship, the government has approved a scheme to push piped gas into many more homes from September 1.
body: About 60 per cent of Indian households cook on LPG, the gas that arrives in a red steel cylinder. Before the war, roughly 90 per cent of India's LPG imports came through the Strait of Hormuz. That route is now disrupted, the fuel is being bought from further away, and the price has climbed.

On Wednesday the government approved an incentive scheme for piped natural gas, starting September 1. Piped gas, or PNG, comes through a pipe in the wall, like water. City gas companies will get an extra 200 cubic metres of cheaper Indian-produced gas for every new household connection they switch on, across two rounds over six months.
The idea is substitution: a fuel India ships in is swapped, kitchen by kitchen, for one it pumps up at home.
india.why: Energy security is not about having energy. It is about how many different ways you can get it. A country with one supplier and one sea route has no choices on the day that route closes. A country with pipelines, several ports and its own gas fields has a few. India is spending money now to buy itself options later.
also: Coking coal prices have jumped about 25 per cent, squeezing the country's steelmakers.
An Indian state oil company has won a US licence to return to Venezuela, opening one door as another shuts.

us.headline: Forty Trillion Dollars, and Counting
us.deck: The Treasury's daily tally crossed the line on Wednesday, only five months after it passed $39 trillion.
body: The federal debt is the total of everything the US government has borrowed and not yet paid back. On Wednesday the Treasury's daily update put it above $40 trillion for the first time, five months after it passed $39 trillion.

Debt grows when a government spends more than it collects, and this year spending is running more than $2 trillion ahead of revenue. Some of that gap is recent: after the Supreme Court struck down many of President Trump's tariffs, the Treasury had to refund more than $100 billion in import taxes collected unlawfully.
Interest on the debt now costs more than $1 trillion a year, the government's second largest expense behind Social Security.

us.why: Governments are not households. They can borrow at sizes no family could. But the bill still arrives. Lenders have been demanding more interest to keep lending, and the yield on 30-year Treasury bonds hit a 19-year high this week. Mortgage rates follow those bonds, so the government's borrowing turns up in what a family pays for a house.
us.analyst: Think like an analyst: a number is only big compared with something. You could measure $40 trillion against the size of the American economy, against a year's tax collection, or against the population, about 340 million people. Work that last one out. Then decide which comparison belongs in a headline, and what each one hides.

items: China: Hui Ka Yan, who built the property giant Evergrande and was once China's richest man, was sentenced to life in prison for fraud and bribery.
Ukraine: a Russian assault on Kyiv overnight killed at least 13 people as talk of peace negotiations goes on.

items.def: Rules one government writes to stop its people and firms trading with another country. Today: Washington wants others to copy its rules on Iran.
The gap left when a government spends more in a year than it collects. Today: US spending is over $2 trillion ahead of revenue.
The rent you pay for borrowed money. Today: the US government pays more than $1 trillion a year in interest alone.
The share of people with a confirmed disease who die of it. Today: about 47 per cent in Congo, 70 per cent in North Kivu.

did_you_know.text: Numbers that look alike can be wildly different sizes. A million seconds is about eleven and a half days. A billion seconds is about thirty-one years and eight months. A trillion seconds is about 31,700 years, reaching back into the last Ice Age, to the people who painted the caves at Chauvet in France.

sports.title: India hold England, and hold their nerve
sports.body: India drew 0-0 with England on Thursday, finishing second in Pool D and reaching the second round of the women's Hockey World Cup. It was defending rather than dazzling: 28 English circle entries and 12 penalty corners survived, with goalkeeper Bichu Devi repeatedly in the way.

items: Whether Washington extends the waiver allowing Iranian oil sales. It expires August 21.
Whether China's banks, Iran's last big buyers, respond to the threat at all.
